paragraphs: This paper studies how reliably a measured area under the ROC curve, or AUC, reflects a ranking function’s expected performance. The setting is bipartite ranking, where the goal is to order examples belonging to two classes. A high score on a finite test set is useful only if it provides dependable information about performance beyond that set.

The authors derive a distribution-free large deviation bound: a mathematical control on how far the measured AUC can depart from its expected value. The bound uses an independent test sequence and does not require specifying a particular data distribution. It therefore connects an observed ranking score with a probabilistic statement about its accuracy.

Comparing this bound with a corresponding classification-error bound suggests that estimating ranking performance requires more test examples for the same accuracy and confidence. The authors also extend the result to ranking functions selected from a finite class, using a union bound to account for the available choices.
neurips-2004-a-large-deviation-bound-for.tldr: The paper bounds uncertainty in empirical AUC and suggests that estimating ranking performance needs more test data than estimating classification error.

paragraphs: The paper develops a system that reconstructs hand movement from neural activity while explicitly tracking how movement evolves over time. Its internal state contains hand position, velocity, and acceleration, and its incoming measurements are instantaneous neural spike rates. The task is therefore to recover a changing trajectory from a stream of neural observations.

Each state estimate combines two contributions: a linear transformation of the previous estimated state and a kernel-based mapping designed to model neural activity. This allows earlier movement estimates and current neural signals to inform the next prediction together. The activity-to-state mapping is trained directly with a loss function designed to be robust to noise.

The authors test the approach using motor-cortex activity from behaving monkeys. In those experiments, it predicts hand trajectories more accurately than both static support vector regression and a Kalman filter. These findings support the usefulness of combining temporal state information with a learned kernel mapping for the evaluated neural decoding task.
neurips-2004-a-temporal-kernel-based-mod.tldr: A temporal kernel model combines previous movement estimates with neural spike rates to improve hand-trajectory prediction in monkey recordings.

paragraphs: This paper addresses object tracking when the appearance of both the target and its surroundings changes over time. A tracker needs a representation that separates the object from the background, but a distinction learned earlier can become less useful as lighting or pose changes. The proposed model adapts that distinction as tracking proceeds.

The authors introduce a discriminative generative model that extends Fisher Linear Discriminant and gives the resulting approach a probabilistic interpretation. In the tracking application, the model is chosen to distinguish target appearance from background appearance. A computationally efficient update algorithm repeatedly revises the model to reflect changes in both.

Experiments show that the method can learn models useful for tracking objects through substantial pose and lighting changes. The central contribution is the combination of discrimination, probabilistic modeling, and continuing adaptation. Rather than treating the initial appearance model as sufficient throughout a sequence, the approach makes learning the changing target-background relationship part of the tracking process.
neurips-2004-adaptive-discriminative-gen.tldr: An efficiently updated probabilistic model adapts the distinction between target and background to track objects through appearance changes.

paragraphs: Online mechanism design studies sequential decisions involving self-interested participants in an uncertain environment. The objective is to maximize value even when participants have reasons to act strategically. This paper examines what happens when the decision problem is too large to solve exactly and the mechanism must use an approximation.

The difficulty is that approximation affects more than computational cost. It may create opportunities for a participant to benefit by misrepresenting information. Building on an approach based on Markov decision processes, the authors use sparse-sampling algorithms to construct policies that are approximately efficient while retaining truthful reporting as an approximate Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

The equilibrium qualification matters: the stated result preserves an approximate incentive property, rather than making an unrestricted claim that manipulation can never help. The authors illustrate the method through dynamic allocation of WiFi connectivity among coffeehouse users. The contribution connects practical approximation of sequential planning with the strategic requirements that make a mechanism usable among self-interested agents.
neurips-2004-approximately-efficient-onl.tldr: Sparse-sampling planning enables approximately efficient online mechanisms while preserving truthful reporting as an approximate Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the dynamics of a recurrent network relate to its ability to compute with time series. The networks consist of randomly connected threshold gates. The authors focus on the boundary between ordered and chaotic behavior, asking whether that transition identifies networks with particularly useful computational properties.

They propose a complexity measure and find that it reaches its highest values near this boundary. They also report that the measure predicts computational capability well. Within the network setting studied, complex time-series computations are possible only near the transition, tying the dynamical regime to the kinds of temporal processing the networks can perform.

The paper additionally presents and analyzes a simple synaptic scaling rule for self-organized criticality. This adds a mechanism for adjusting network connections toward the relevant dynamical condition to the analysis of why that condition matters. Together, the results connect a measurable property of network dynamics, observed computational capacity, and a rule for organizing the network’s operating regime.
neurips-2004-at-the-edge-of-chaos-real-t.tldr: For the studied recurrent threshold networks, a complexity measure peaks near the edge of chaos and predicts time-series computational ability.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a decision-making system can commit to several activities at once. Each activity is represented as an action that extends over time in a semi-Markov decision process. The planning problem is to combine activities while respecting a hierarchy in which subordinate activities must fit the requirements of superior ones.

Instead of assigning each activity one fixed policy, the method defines a set of admissible solutions. This set includes alternative optimal policies and policies that move upward along the activity’s optimal state-value function. Keeping multiple acceptable ways to carry out an activity gives the planner room to accommodate other commitments.

The planner merges these solution sets so that subordinate activities are realized within the admissible solutions of superior activities. The authors provide theoretical results and evaluate the approach in a simulated domain. The central idea is that simultaneous commitments can be organized through flexibility in acceptable policies, rather than requiring every activity to follow one independently fixed course of action.
neurips-2004-coarticulation-in-markov-de.tldr: The paper combines temporally extended activities by fitting subordinate policies within the admissible solutions of higher-priority activities.

paragraphs: This paper compares methods for solving 3-SAT, the problem of finding truth assignments that satisfy a collection of three-variable clauses. It first develops a shared derivation of survey propagation, belief propagation, and hybrid methods using probability arguments. This places several approaches within a common framework for examining their relationships.

The authors then use the random-walk solver WSAT to assess formula difficulty, both before and after simplification guided by survey propagation. Their numerical experiments examine how difficulty varies with formula parameters. At a fixed ratio of clauses to variables, WSAT’s mean cost grows proportionally with the number of variables in the easy satisfiable regime and somewhat beyond it.

In the hard satisfiable regime, WSAT’s behavior appears to reflect solution-space structure predicted by replica symmetry-breaking arguments. This is presented as an observed correspondence. The comparison of search tradeoffs indicates that WSAT is more powerful than previously appreciated and motivates further practical algorithm development alongside the unified probabilistic treatment of propagation methods.
neurips-2004-comparing-beliefs-surveys-a.tldr: A unified probabilistic treatment of propagation methods and numerical comparisons reveal underappreciated strengths of the random-walk SAT solver WSAT.

paragraphs: The paper aims to make support vector decision functions faster to evaluate for object detection. Detection can require scanning large images, so the cost of repeatedly applying the decision function matters. The starting point is an existing approximation that replaces the original support vectors with a smaller collection of synthesized points in the input space.

The authors change how those replacement points are constructed. Instead of allowing unconstrained optimization, they impose a structural restriction that makes the resulting approximation evaluable using separable filters. Thus, the method reduces computational effort through the form of the replacement points as well as through the smaller size of the set.

In face-detection experiments, the rank-deficient approximations run four to six times faster than unconstrained reduced-set systems. This result directly supports the computational value of the structural constraint in the tested application. The broader contribution is an approximation strategy that takes the eventual cost of scanning images into account when constructing a faster decision function.
neurips-2004-face-detection-efficient-an.tldr: Structurally constrained support-vector approximations enable separable filtering and achieve four-to-sixfold speedups over unconstrained reduced-set systems in face detection.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction in a matrix for which only some entries have been observed. Its approach fits those observations with a low-rank matrix and uses that fit to predict other entries. The central question is whether agreement with the available entries provides a reliable basis for predictions beyond them.

The authors prove generalization-error bounds for this procedure. Such bounds address the gap between fitting the observed data and performing well on entries to be predicted. The contribution therefore supplies theoretical support for using a low-rank restriction in collaborative prediction, connecting the chosen model structure to control of prediction error.

The analysis also includes a caution about measuring the complexity of function classes. The authors construct a class with finite pseudodimension whose sums have unbounded pseudodimension. This shows that a finite complexity measure for the component class does not, by itself, guarantee the same property for sums. The example helps justify the analytical approach used to obtain the matrix-prediction bounds.
neurips-2004-generalization-error-bounds.tldr: The paper proves generalization bounds for low-rank matrix prediction and shows why finite component pseudodimension alone cannot control sums.

paragraphs: Some decision rules inspect cues one at a time and stop as soon as a cue settles the choice. This can save information and computation, but the order of inspection matters greatly. The paper asks whether choosing that order can also be simple, rather than becoming the expensive part of an otherwise economical decision process.

The motivation comes from Take The Best, which orders cues by validity. Computing that ordering can require substantial work and potentially weaken the computational advantage of the decision rule. Because several cue orders can support good decisions, the authors investigate simpler ordering mechanisms drawn partly from sequential searches through data records.

They examine tallying, swapping, and move-to-front rules, and show that these mechanisms can produce orders with reasonable accuracy and substantial savings in cue use. The result supports treating cue ordering as part of the overall cost of decision-making. An inexpensive ordering procedure can preserve useful performance without requiring the ordering itself to be computationally elaborate.
neurips-2004-heuristics-for-ordering-cue.tldr: Simple cue-ordering rules can support reasonably accurate decisions while preserving the information savings of stopping at the first decisive cue.

paragraphs: This paper develops a visual tracker that learns its representation of the target while tracking it. The motivation is that lighting, pose, and viewing angle can change the object’s appearance after tracking begins. A compact representation that adapts to those changes can remain useful as new observations arrive.

The method incrementally updates a low-dimensional eigenspace representation. A specific contribution is that it updates both the sample mean and the eigenbasis, accounting for the fact that the average observed appearance changes over time. The authors contrast this with incremental subspace methods that neglect the changing mean.

Tracking is formulated as state inference within a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework, with a particle filter carrying sample distributions forward over time. Experiments in indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate effectiveness when targets undergo large pose and lighting changes. The paper brings together evolving appearance learning and temporal state inference, making adaptation of the target model an ongoing part of the tracking procedure.
neurips-2004-incremental-learning-for-vi.tldr: An online visual tracker adapts a compact appearance model by updating both its mean and eigenbasis as the target changes.

paragraphs: The paper brings together two kinds of statistical structure in language: nearby word relationships associated with syntax and longer-range relationships associated with meaning. Statistical language-learning approaches often emphasize one of these sources of information. The authors ask whether a single generative model can use both to discover useful linguistic organization.

Their model simultaneously identifies syntactic classes and semantic topics through statistical dependencies. It does not require an additional representation of syntax or semantics beyond those dependencies. This makes the joint treatment central to the approach: local and long-range patterns both contribute to the structure the model learns.

The model is competitive on tasks including part-of-speech tagging and document classification when compared with models focused on the corresponding short-range or long-range information. The finding indicates that integrating the two dependency scales can retain useful performance on both kinds of task. Its significance is the ability to learn grammatical and topical organization together within one statistical modeling framework.
neurips-2004-integrating-topics-and-synt.tldr: A single generative model learns syntactic classes and semantic topics jointly from short- and long-range word dependencies.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how individual participants contribute to the pattern of turn-taking in conversation. The authors collect auditory recordings through wearable sensors from twenty-three people, with sixty-six hours per person over two weeks. Automated speech and conversation detection identifies conversations, their participants, and who is speaking at each point.

They model paired turn-taking with a Mixed-Memory Markov Model. The model combines statistics describing each person’s own transitions with cross-transitions involving the conversational partner. Its mixture parameters express the contribution of individual behavior to the pair’s joint behavior, providing an estimated measure of conversational influence.

The estimated influence correlates significantly with betweenness centrality, a separate measure of a person’s importance in a social network. This association suggests that conversational influence may predict social influence. The result connects the fine-grained timing of speech with a broader network property, while the model gives a quantitative interpretation to how the two participants shape their shared turn-taking pattern.
neurips-2004-modeling-conversational-dyn.tldr: A mixed-memory model estimates influence from conversational turn-taking, and those estimates correlate with social-network betweenness centrality.

paragraphs: This paper tackles object classification when only one example of a target class is available. Learning directly from so little data can overfit. The proposed solution uses examples from related classes to learn which aspects of an object representation should matter when measuring similarity.

The method follows two stages. First, it learns a distance metric from related classes. Then it applies nearest-neighbor classification to the single examples using that metric. The motivating condition is sufficient for perfect classification: every within-class distance must be smaller than every between-class distance. The framework seeks a metric that achieves this separation; the conditional argument does not establish that every learned metric will do so.

Because linear projections may be unable to emphasize the needed dimensions, the authors use kernel-based metric learning. Objects are represented as sets of local descriptors with an appropriate image kernel. Demonstrations on synthetic data and character classification illustrate the strategy of transferring a useful notion of similarity before learning from a single example.
neurips-2004-object-classification-from-.tldr: The framework learns a kernel-based similarity metric from related classes, then uses it for nearest-neighbor classification from single examples.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a hardware obstacle to learning in analog neural networks: nominally similar devices can behave differently. These mismatches reduce the accuracy of analog arithmetic circuits, which in turn lowers the learning performance of networks built from them. The problem therefore links physical circuit variation to the quality of the network’s learning.

The authors present compact calibration techniques implemented on the chip itself. The techniques use little power and compensate for device mismatch. Their stated capability is to enable large-scale analog VLSI neural networks with learning performance on the order of ten bits, connecting correction of circuit behavior with useful computational precision.

The techniques are demonstrated on a fabricated linear perceptron with sixty-four synapses, trained using the Least-Mean-Squares algorithm. This gives a concrete hardware setting for the calibration approach. The contribution is a way to address mismatch within the analog implementation, so that device variation need not determine learning accuracy to the same extent as it would without compensation.
neurips-2004-on-chip-compensation-of-dev.tldr: Compact, low-power on-chip calibration compensates for analog device mismatch and supports learning performance on the order of ten bits.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to simplify a graphical model while preserving its probability distribution as well as possible. It searches a specified class of subgraphs for the one that is optimal under KL divergence. The goal is therefore a principled choice of reduced model, with optimality defined relative to the allowed subgraph class.

The authors introduce a decomposition-tree representation closely related to a junction tree and use it to compute the optimal subgraph. Their approach extends graph-separation techniques previously used for combinatorial optimization. For some important subgraph classes, the extension works even when the original graph’s minimal separators are arbitrarily large.

The stated applications include finding an optimal model over a (k − 1)-tree within a model over a k-tree, and optimally removing a constant number of edges. The formulation gives polynomial-time solutions in the number of vertices for these problems. The significance is that useful optimal simplifications remain computationally accessible beyond settings requiring small minimal separators.
neurips-2004-optimal-sub-graphical-model.tldr: A decomposition-tree method finds KL-optimal subgraphical models for important classes, including cases with arbitrarily large minimal separators.

paragraphs: The paper derives a learning rule for a spiking neuron from the objective of maximizing mutual information. This gives the rule a specified sense of optimality: it is tied to information transmission in the neuron model. The authors use that objective to investigate how learning should depend on spike timing.

Under the assumption that input fluctuations are small, the derivation produces a spike-timing dependent plasticity function. Its form depends on the time course of excitatory postsynaptic potentials and on the postsynaptic neuron’s autocorrelation function. The learning rule thus reflects both the response to excitatory input and the temporal structure of the neuron’s own activity.

The resulting timing function has positive and negative phases. The positive phase is related to the excitatory potential’s shape, while the negative phase is governed by neuronal refractoriness. These results provide an information-based explanation for the two phases within the stated model and small-fluctuation assumption, linking the shape of plasticity to particular aspects of neuronal dynamics.
neurips-2004-spike-timing-dependent-plas.tldr: Under small input fluctuations, information maximization yields a spike-timing learning rule whose positive and negative phases reflect excitation and refractoriness.

paragraphs: This paper examines access consciousness: why some mental states are available for evaluation, choice, and verbal report while others are not. It considers two proposed requirements, the quality of a representation and the ability to communicate it. The authors introduce a probabilistic information transmission model that suggests both requirements are essential.

The model had previously accounted for repetition-priming data. Here, the authors apply it to findings from two subliminal-priming experiments. The important behavior is that prior information can affect subsequent processing even when the relevant internal states are not accessible or reportable.

The model reproduces priming without accessibility and reportability, providing a mechanism for separating the effect of a mental state from conscious access to that state. This allows the two proposed requirements for access to be considered together in a working account of the experimental findings. The contribution is a model-based explanation of how priming and awareness can come apart, with representation quality and communication both playing a role.
neurips-2004-theories-of-access-consciou.tldr: A probabilistic information-transmission model explains subliminal priming while suggesting that conscious access requires both representation quality and communication.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a model can predict consumers’ sensory impressions of beef from descriptions of the meat. A key complication is that ratings express preferences among products encountered in the same testing session. The learning problem therefore needs to account for the comparative context in which those judgments are made.

The authors use a support vector machine with a specially designed polynomial kernel for this task. Their training data include ratings from expert and consumer panels, using meat from 103 cattle across seven Spanish breeds. The samples vary in carcass weight and aging period, giving the model several traits to relate to appreciation.

The study also uses feature-subset selection to identify which traits matter for consumer preferences. Aging emerges as the most important trait for improving appreciation in the reported analysis. The contribution combines prediction with interpretation: the model addresses the structure of sensory ratings, while selecting traits yields an actionable finding about what distinguishes more appreciated beef in this study.
neurips-2004-trait-selection-for-assessi.tldr: A specialized nonlinear SVM models beef preferences, and feature selection identifies aging as the most important trait in the study.

paragraphs: This paper defines surprise in terms of how an observation changes an observer’s beliefs. The quantity compares beliefs before and after receiving data, making surprise depend on the effect of the data on the observer. The authors characterize this Bayesian definition as the only consistent formulation under their minimal axiomatic assumptions.

They use the framework to investigate where people look while watching television and video games. Across the measured gaze shifts, seventy-two percent go toward locations whose surprise exceeds the average. When considering gaze targets selected simultaneously by all subjects, the proportion rises to eighty-four percent.

These findings show a strong relationship between the proposed surprise measure and gaze allocation in the studied viewing conditions. The mathematical definition also offers a common way to describe surprise across spatial and temporal scales, sensory modalities, and levels of abstraction. The paper connects that broad formulation to observed attention by testing whether changes in modeled beliefs correspond to the places that attract viewers’ eyes.
neurips-2005-bayesian-surprise-attracts-.tldr: Bayesian surprise measures belief change, and the study finds that human gaze shifts strongly favor locations scored as more surprising.

paragraphs: This paper identifies two problems in spectral graph partitioning, a method for splitting graphs using a spectral embedding. The first concerns turning that embedding into an actual cut. The authors argue that commonly used hyperplane rounding tends to miss the best cuts because of how the embedding represents them.

They recommend flow-based rounding to address this problem. The second weakness concerns balance: for many power-law graphs, spectral partitioning produces parts of very unequal size. Such cuts reduce its usefulness for visualization and divide-and-conquer algorithms, even though the usual quotient-style objective already encourages some balance.

The authors address this second problem with a stricter balance constraint. This changes the mathematical formulation into a semidefinite program that can be solved for million-node graphs using the cited optimization method. The contribution separates two sources of poor partitions and gives a corresponding remedy for each: improve how the embedding is rounded, and explicitly strengthen the requirement that the resulting partition be balanced.
neurips-2005-fixing-two-weaknesses-of-th.tldr: Flow-based rounding and a stricter balance constraint address missed cuts and unbalanced partitions in spectral graph methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to learn correspondences between different kinds of observations. Its algorithm uses Gaussian process regression and connects the observation spaces through a single lower-dimensional latent space. That hidden space represents structure shared by the corresponding observations, providing a common basis for relating otherwise heterogeneous measurements.

The authors demonstrate the method on two datasets. In the first application, it learns nonlinear relationships between corresponding views of objects. These learned relationships support synthesis of new views, with missing data filled in as needed. The shared representation therefore serves as a basis for generating observations as well as linking existing ones.

In the second application, the method relates human degrees of freedom to those of a humanoid robot. This enables imitation of human poses from motion-capture data. Together, the results illustrate how learning common hidden structure can support synthesis across different observation spaces, including visual views and human-to-robot pose correspondences, within the same proposed algorithm.
neurips-2005-learning-shared-latent-stru.tldr: A shared latent space learned with Gaussian processes supports novel-view synthesis and mapping human motion-capture poses to a humanoid robot.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much experience cooperative reinforcement learning requires as the number of agents grows. Its focus is the number of real-world examples needed for good performance. In a large distributed system, that requirement can determine whether learning is practical even when agents share a common objective.

The authors prove a worst-case lower bound for algorithms that learn policies solely from a global reward signal. For those algorithms, the required number of examples scales roughly linearly with the number of agents. This establishes a fundamental limitation of relying only on that shared feedback in the worst case.

They also identify a class of algorithms that uses local reward signals in large distributed Markov decision processes and guarantees good performance with sample requirements scaling as O(log n). This result shows how the form of feedback can change the scaling of learning. The logarithmic guarantee applies to the described algorithm class and setting, giving a route to learning with very many agents.
neurips-2005-on-local-rewards-and-scalin.tldr: Global-reward-only learning has a roughly linear worst-case sample requirement, while a class using local rewards achieves logarithmic scaling.

paragraphs: The paper extends compressed sensing from individual sparse signals to collections of related signals. Its goal is to reconstruct multiple signals from small sets of linear projections while taking advantage of structure both within each signal and across the collection. The authors call this framework distributed compressed sensing.

The central concept is joint sparsity, which describes useful sparse structure at the level of a signal ensemble. The paper studies three simple models of that structure and proposes algorithms that recover several signals together from incoherent projections. Joint recovery makes the relationships among signals part of the reconstruction procedure.

The authors analyze, both theoretically and empirically, how many measurements each sensor needs for accurate reconstruction. This connects the structural models to concrete measurement requirements. The framework is presented as applicable to sensor networks and arrays, where multiple sources can carry related information. Its contribution is to organize distributed compression and recovery around shared sparse structure rather than treating each source entirely separately.
neurips-2005-recovery-of-jointly-sparse-.tldr: Distributed compressed sensing uses joint sparsity to reconstruct related signals together and characterize the measurements required per sensor.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model of bottom-up overt attention: the allocation of gaze driven by properties of a visual scene. Its guiding principle is to maximize the information sampled from that scene. The model uses Shannon’s self-information measure to turn this principle into a saliency computation.

The authors describe how the proposed operation can be carried out by a neural circuit and demonstrate close connections with circuitry in the primate visual cortex. This connects the information-based objective to a possible neural implementation. They also show that the saliency measure may be extended to address issues that existing saliency models have difficulty explaining.

The model is evaluated on natural images by comparing its predictions with experimental eye-tracking data and existing approaches. The reported results support its effectiveness in predicting where overt attention is directed. The contribution brings together an information-maximization principle, a circuit-level account, and behavioral evaluation, using the same saliency formulation to connect what is informative in an image with where viewers look.
neurips-2005-saliency-based-on-informati.tldr: An information-maximizing saliency model links a neural circuit formulation with successful prediction of gaze allocation in natural images.
